articles.title: Trump puts on hold new Russia sanctions he signed into law - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Trump puts on hold new Russia sanctions he signed into law  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia that he signed into law last month, telling Congress the pause is in the national interest.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday, two days before a deadline in the law that would put the sanctions into effect.
The law – named after Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator who died unexpectedly in July after returning from Ukraine – passed in the House of Representatives and the Senate by large margins. The bipartisan legislation was drafted by Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.
It seeks to starve Moscow of money for its war on Ukraine by sanctioning Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers carrying its energy exports.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas with an exception for countries that import less than 15 percent of Russia’s natural gas exports and are taking steps to cut them.
Kirill Dmitriev, special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on social media that Trump’s move was “an important and truly historic moment”.
“The US-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue,” he added.
Diesel deal and criticism
The decision to suspend the sanctions came a week after Trump said the US signed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to try to lower global fuel prices.
Both Republicans and Democrats criticised the deal, saying it would help Russia’s war effort without affecting fuel prices.
Democratic Representative Don Beyer said he and other politicians had “warned” that Trump might do this, referring to Trump’s deal with Moscow.
Beyer called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine”.
Trump recently has also increasingly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to reach a deal with Russia.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Oleksandr Merezhko, the chairman of the Ukrainian parliament’s Committee on Foreign Policy and Interparliamentary Cooperation, linked Trump’s latest moves, which put Ukraine at a disadvantage, to next month’s midterm elections in the US and predicted an improvement in relations after the voting.
“President Trump is a difficult partner, but we are dependent on the United States, and we need to have constructive, respectful relations even with Trump, no matter how difficult it might be,” he said.
“I believe that after the midterm elections, the situation will be better, the emotions will subside and we will be able to return to constructive dialogue with President Trump,” Merezhko added.
Polls have suggested that Trump’s Republican Party will have a hard time keeping its majorities in Congress in the November 3 elections due to voters disapproving of Trump’s handling of the US-Israel war on Iran and blaming him for higher prices.

articles.title: Trump calls for end to Russia-Ukraine war amid Zelenskyy's warning against trusting Putin - www.malaysiasun.com
articles.summary: Trump calls for end to Russia-Ukraine war amid Zelenskyy's warning against trusting Putin  www.malaysiasun.com
articles.full_text:
ANI
                
17 Oct 2026, 02:27 GMT+10
            
Washington DC [US], October 17 (ANI): US President Donald Trump on Friday (local time) said he wanted the Russia-Ukraine war to end, claiming that both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wanted an end to the conflict, even as the Ukrainian leader accused Moscow of showing no genuine willingness to negotiate.
Speaking to reporters ahead of a rally in Georgia, Trump was asked whether he had forgotten that Putin started the war.
'Well, you know, I know the details, okay? And at some point, I'll release the details. But I don't care anything except for one. I want that war ended. 25,000 soldiers on average a month are being killed. Last month, it was 32,000 soldiers. And I think the two leaders, I deal with both of them. I think they want that war ended, too, and I think it's going to end. That's all I care about. I want that war to end,' Trump said.
However, Zelenskyy said Russia had shown no signs of readiness to end the conflict, accusing Putin of using rhetoric that did not reflect a genuine desire for peace.
Following a conversation with media representatives in Brussels, Zelenskyy said in a post on X, 'Putin doesn't want negotiations right now - in any format. He's playing word games, saying that "they're responding." It looks like a travesty of any genuine desire to end the war.'
The Ukrainian President also warned against easing sanctions on Russia, saying concessions over energy deals could lead to broader sanctions relief.
'We can't accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next. I'm absolutely sure of that. After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don't defend that through diplomacy - who will do it for us?' he said.
Zelenskyy further accused Putin of seeking to undermine Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, questioning whether Russia's ambitions would be limited to eastern Ukraine.
'Putin wants to destroy us. He doesn't respect us, our sovereignty and territorial integrity. He really thinks that we are not a country, not a nation. Do you really believe that just the eastern part of our country will be enough for him? Then why did he go for Kyiv when the full-scale invasion began? Is that Donbas? No, it's the capital. Without the capital, there is no state,' he said.
He also warned that Russian drone activity posed a wider security risk to Europe, including NATO members, and cautioned against underestimating the threat.
'And what will happen afterwards? On what borders will he stay? If now he's testing all these drones against European, even NATO countries? They are not loud for now. They don't want to escalate because they have one Russian drone, two drones, ten. But you will be very loud when there will be ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and thousands of drones. We had one thousand drones yesterday,' Zelenskyy said.
Meanwhile, Putin praised Russian military strikes against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities and logistics centres, according to Russia's state-run TASS news agency.
During a visit to an auxiliary command post of the Joint Force on October 16, Putin claimed Russian forces were advancing along the frontline and had captured more than 1,300 square kilometres of territory in Donbas and Novorossiya in September.
'The Chief of the General Staff has already noted in his report that the military units have achieved a rapid pace of advance. As has already been mentioned here, in September alone, more than 1,300 square kilometers of territory in Donbass and Novorossiya have been liberated,' Putin said.
Putin also called for stronger air defence to protect civilian and military facilities, acknowledging that there was room to improve the effectiveness of Russian air defence crews.
'Overall, air defense combat crews are operating professionally. But, of course, there is room for improvement in this regard. We need to enhance the effectiveness of our defense of civilian, first and foremost civilian, and, of course, military facilities,' he said.
He ruled out discussing the establishment of a security zone along Russia's border territories during potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.
'Our task is to ensure absolute security of Russia's border territories in the future and we are not going to make this a subject of any potential peace talks with Ukraine,' Putin said.
The statements come amid continued hostilities and disagreements over negotiations, sanctions and the conditions for ending the war.
Earlier, Zelenskyy met European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to seek further European assistance for Ukraine's energy infrastructure, air defence and financial resilience.
On October 15, Zelenskyy declared an end to Ukraine's pause on strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, accusing Moscow of violating the US-announced energy ceasefire. Trump had announced the immediate energy ceasefire on October 11, calling on both sides to stop targeting energy infrastructure.
The arrangement came under strain after Zelenskyy accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities, which he said had damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted electricity supplies. (ANI)

articles.title: 'Important ally and partner': Rubio leaves for India amid Trump’s Russian oil tariff threat - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'Important ally and partner': Rubio leaves for India amid Trump’s Russian oil tariff threat  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
US secretary of state 
Marco Rubio
 has departed for India amid a temporary pause in President 
Donald Trump
’s tariff threat over Russian oil purchases, with energy cooperation, trade and strategic ties expected to dominate his October 20 visit.
According to new agency ANI, Rubio departed from Joint Base Andrews late on Saturday (local time) for Uzbekistan and India. “Just departed for Uzbekistan and India to continue securing the Trump Administration's economic opportunities for our nation,” he said ahead of his departure.
The visit comes after Trump paused key provisions of the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which could have imposed tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the US from major buyers of Russian oil, including India and China.
The 60-day pause is intended to give Washington time to assess the potential impact of the proposed measures on the global and US economies.
Rubio defended the decision to reassess the proposed measures, saying India’s energy requirements and its strategic importance to Washington needed to be considered before imposing tariffs and sanctions.
“These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others. 
And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said.
He acknowledged that India had diversified its energy sources but continued to rely substantially on Russian supplies, making an immediate shift difficult.

During his October 20 visit, Rubio is scheduled to meet External affairs minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai to strengthen the bilateral strategic partnership and discuss energy, trade, investment, defence and critical and emerging technologies.
He is also expected to travel to Jamnagar in Gujarat on October 21 to meet Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani and other company officials at the refinery hub, as Washington seeks to expand energy cooperation and commercial ties with India.
India’s ministry of external affairs said the visit would provide an opportunity to review bilateral relations and advance the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership between the two countries.
Before arriving in India, Rubio will attend the C5+1 ministerial meeting in Uzbekistan, focusing on strategic cooperation between the United States and Central Asian countries.

articles.title: Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Samarkand, the fabled Silk Road city in what is now central Uzbekistan, for talks with key regional ministers on Saturday.
The C5+1 – Central Asia plus the US – summit to be held from Saturday to Tuesday heralds Washington’s new approach to the ex-Soviet region – pragmatic, purely transactional and devoid of speeches about democratisation and human rights.
Recommended Stories
At the dawn of Central Asia’s independence, Americans used to show up in the mostly Muslim region strategically stretched between Russia, China and Iran, bearing gifts – and giving lectures.
After the 1991 Soviet collapse, amid the region’s economic degradation, joblessness and poverty, US and European diplomats and businessmen were seen as ambassadors of the brave new world of capitalist prosperity.
They wanted reforms – and not just the economic ones.
Western diplomats made sure that former Communist apparatchiks-turned-new regional leaders understood that they’d get investments, technologies and international recognition only in exchange for abandoning the Soviet-era totalitarian ways of governing and building the economy.
The West held forums and workshops on human rights, democracy and decentralisation of governance, and sent thousands of students and officials to Western schools.
And the West accused regional leaders of losing their moral compass and threatened sanctions when they began to amend their nation’s constitutions to extend their presidential terms, appoint their family members and friends to key government jobs and help them create business empires that often competed with Western investors.
“When the West began moralising, teaching them about democracy, human rights, they immediately turned towards China or Russia,” Galiya Ibragimova, Uzbekistan-born, Moldova-based regional expert, told Al Jazeera.
Uzbekistan, the region’s most populous nation of 37 million, offers a perfect example.
Its iron-fisted President Islam Karimov was the first ex-Soviet leader to allow a US military base on its soil in 2001.
But four years later, he kicked it out after Washington lambasted his brutal suppression of a popular revolt in the eastern city of Andijan that killed hundreds of unarmed civilians.
In 2005, a leaked US diplomatic cable called Karimov’s daughter, Gulnara, a “robber baron” who forcibly took over lucrative businesses and was seen as her father’s successor.
Turning to Russia
As to moralising and lecturing, the tables have turned since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, observers say.
Moscow still has plenty of soft power in Central Asia – from movies and pop music to theatre festivals and propagandist TV shows that constantly lie about the war.
The Kremlin also uses its economic clout to promote the imperialist concept of the “Russian World”, where the region is seen as Moscow’s “near abroad”, and its pre-Russian heritage is snubbed as backwards and insignificant.
In 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Kazakhstan had “never had statehood”, and his ideological allies repeatedly threatened to annex its Russian-speaking northern part.
This year, Kazakhstan began extraditing Kremlin critics and supplying gas to Russia amid Ukrainian drone attacks on its oil refineries.
In January, Kremlin propagandist Vladimir Solovyov said Moscow should launch a “special military operation” – a term reserved for the war in Ukraine – in Central Asia and Armenia.
Critical remarks from minor political figures followed – but no rebukes from the halls of real power.
Meanwhile, Central Asian labour migrants have been duped or forced into enlisting to fight in Ukraine in droves, while Moscow uses Central Asian companies to import microchips, communications equipment and machine tools to build drones and missiles.
“These days, the US and Russia have switched roles. Today, it’s Russia that began building ties through moralising,” Ibragimova, the regional expert, said.
Return of the White House?
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump’s administration has abandoned the pro-democracy stance and now advocates a utilitarian, transactional approach to foreign policy.
“Under Trump, the American policy in Central Asia is all about ‘just business and nothing more’, without being nosy about human rights, reforms. They are content with everything,” Ibragimova said.
Earlier this month, Trump received Saida Mirziyoyeva, the daughter of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
A year earlier, Mirziyoyev pledged to invest up to $100bn in the US economy, buy Boeing aircraft and even US-grown cotton, even though Uzbekistan is one of the world’s largest cotton growers.
Washington did not say a word about Mirziyoyev’s crackdown on critics or his daughter’s growing domestic clout.
After largely ignoring Central Asia during Trump’s first term, the White House wants to resume its presence.
“The interest is mostly geopolitical and military-strategic, considering the region’s location in the zone of Russia’s and China’s interests,” Alisher Ilkhamov, head of the London-based Central Asia Due Diligence think tank, told Al Jazeera.
“In the future, Washington apparently wants to have a military base here as a deterrent measure against China,” he said.
The economic interests seem to be focused on rare-earth minerals – crucial for manufacturing a wide array of technology – and other critical elements, especially since China uses them as a political cudgel in its ties with Washington.
The deposits are abundant, but need development, technologies and investment.
Meanwhile, the White House shows little interest in human rights violations in Central Asia, such as the jailing of political opponents and independent journalists.
“An interest in these issues, unfortunately, is absent from Rubio’s agenda, because these problems went missing from US foreign policy priorities since Trump returned to the White House,” Ilkhamov said.
A Norwegian human rights advocate echoes his concerns.
“There are uncomfortable similarities between Trump’s worldview and established authoritarian regimes like Tajikistan and Turkmenistan,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.
“However, Marco Rubio probably has a better understanding of Central Asia and the challenges there than does [Vice President] JD Vance and [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth,” he said.
The US State Department “should bring back the focus [on human rights] if the C5+1 format is to be taken seriously going forward”, he said.

articles.title: China’s Strategic Reassessment of India - War on the Rocks
articles.summary: China’s Strategic Reassessment of India  War on the Rocks
articles.full_text:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
As China and India have improved their relations in recent months, many observers have attributed this improvement to the end of U.S. strategic altruism toward India. Indeed, in the past year, China has watched India lose its balance and simmer in a sense of strategic disorientation due to America’s change of heart. Delegation after delegation of Indian strategists visited China, trying to mend ties in search of balance in the Chinese view. Many Chinese experts see India as returning to middle-power alignment for “economic authority and strategic freedom,” which translates into vigorous outreach to Europe, Japan, Canada, and all the middle powers. It’s almost as if India is returning to its middle-power roots.
The Chinese reassessment of India’s power status and its strategic malleability — the extent to which its choices can be shaped — and predictability has significant implications for understanding future dynamics between the two powers. The renewed improvement in ties raises questions about its sincerity and limits. While China recalibrates its relations with India, it is also building fences and chokeholds, first and foremost through supply chain dependence. It is unclear what future policy the next U.S. administration will pursue toward either China or India. Both powers therefore keep their options open.
These assessments reflect ongoing research on China’s role in South Asia. They draw on 10 research trips to China, as well as roundtables and exchanges held online and in Washington with Chinese experts since January 2025. China demonstrates a strong tendency toward binary judgments on India’s alignment choice, while the reality is far more nuanced, as U.S. policy should be.
In the Chinese policy discourse on India, the first and foremost question has always been India’s power status: Is India a great power, or is it simply a middle power with great-power potential? While India’s gross domestic product has consistently been a fraction of China’s, its claim to great-power status has had major sway over China’s calculus. Vishwa Guru — “India the world’s guru” — is a famous slogan created under the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi that, in the Chinese view, best represents India’s strategic aspiration: India not only aspires to be a world-class great power but also sees itself as superior and therefore will teach all the other great powers. Although Chinese policymakers do not have romantic misperceptions of India’s actual power status, India’s aspiration and, even more so, its boldness have been no small shock to Chinese policymakers, who follow the tradition of overestimating adversaries’ capacity and hiding their own strength （料敌从宽，判己从严）. India’s bold statement made Beijing question whether it underestimated fundamental aspects of Indian capability and potential that warranted India’s great-power status.
More importantly, during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration, China stopped questioning India’s great-power status. India played a pivotal role in America’s Indo-Pacific strategy during these eight years, to the extent that Washington “hyped India’s power status” （大肆吹捧印度） and “exaggerated India’s development potential.”（夸大其发展潜力）
America’s willingness to elevate India to a global great power and its seemingly endless provision of assistance to lift India up changed China’s original view that only real comprehensive national power mattered. India’s gross domestic product has been only about 20 percent of China’s and has been unlikely to catch up any time soon to become China’s peer. However, that could entirely change if American support continues. Beijing knows this too well because China had been the beneficiary of similar American support and elevation from the 1970s to the 2000s. The difference for China is that back then the United States supported China to counter the Soviet Union, and during the first Trump and Biden administrations, the United States lent similar support to India to counter China. The lesson for China is that great-power status does not actually have to be expressed in real, current terms rather than future expectations and potentials, and U.S. support could very realistically and rapidly elevate India to a new height and single-handedly make India a new great power.
Seeing India as an aspirational and rising power, China believes it followed a policy of accommodation with India throughout this period and beyond. General Secretary Xi Jinping continued outreach and friendly messaging to Modi, including in 2018 (right after the Doklam standoff in 2017); in 2024 at the Kazan summit of the expanded economic bloc originally formed by Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa; and in 2025 when hosting Modi at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit. China did not pursue reciprocal, retaliatory economic policies toward India after 2020. Even on the issue of visas, Chinese officials cited the 280,000 visas China issued to Indian nationals in 2025 to highlight the 2,000 visas India issued to Chinese nationals during the same period to demonstrate the vastly different treatments. For China, these are all reflections of its unwillingness to completely sour ties with India.
But now, with India losing America’s favor, India’s great-power status has become much less persuasive. Chinese strategists are returning to the view that perhaps, after all, India is just a middle power. It has great potential, but elements in the Indian strategic culture pose irremovable obstacles and consistently sabotage its ascension.
As Chinese strategists observe the fluctuation of ties between the United States and India in the past nine years, it is unsettling and reassuring at the same time. The vast scope and depth of what the United States and India could jointly achieve materially and in practice is unsettling for China, exacerbating China’s anxiety about India’s future alignment or alliance with the United States and how it could undermine China’s roles and aspirations. However, the limitations to what the United States could persuade India to do, even with great rewards and strategic benefits promised, are reassuring for Beijing.
For example, despite the favors and support the United States is willing to provide India, India has refused to abandon its strategic autonomy. At the height of the Russo-Ukrainian War and American demand for India to cooperate, India refused to abandon economic and energy ties with Russia. In private conversations, India’s foreign policy community firmly distinguished between “like-minded” and “same-minded” countries to protect its strategic autonomy, and Indian diplomats vehemently emphasized issue-based alignments rather than permanent, rigid alliances.
For China, this is cognitively incomprehensible, as it essentially equates to “India wants to have its cake and eat it, too.” If the United States does not have full confidence in Indian loyalty and support, why would the United States spend its valuable resources to do India the favor and let India run with its own agenda? If the answer is a shared U.S.-Indian aspiration to curtail China’s rise and expansion, India’s expressed reluctance to support the United States and confront China militarily on China’s western flank in a future Taiwan contingency, a position that was reiterated amply in track two dialogues, has certainly made the case of “strategic altruism” less appealing for the United States.
On the drastically different interpretations of U.S. support and Indian reactions, all of the China and India specialists I spoke with refer to the Indian concept of “Dānā” (almsgiving) to explain what they see as India’s “ungratefulness.” What the United States identified as strategic altruism, India sees as strategic egoism because, in Indian culture, the concept of almsgiving views the recipient as doing a favor to the giver by providing them an opportunity to clear negative karma and practice detachment. Following this logic, Indian acceptance of U.S. assistance is India doing the United States a favor, and the United States should be in debt to India consequently. The correctness of this Chinese argument is debatable, but Chinese specialists’ unanimous claim of this cultural reading of a religious tradition as the origin of Indian strategic behavior is certainly noteworthy.
Essentially, China perceives India’s strategic choice as unmalleable, which significantly, or even critically, undercuts India’s potential. Despite the amount of support the United States was willing to supply, India has adhered to its strategic autonomy and refuses to alienate Russia or support a U.S. military campaign against China. Similarly, despite the amount of accommodation China sees itself as willing to provide India, including in economic cooperation, India also adheres to its longstanding position and refuses to forge closer ties. That means India’s strategic choice is predictable and cannot be shaped by the enticement of rewards or the threat of punishments. That substantially reduces the strategic value of India as a U.S. partner in strategic competition with China, and consequently, China’s anxiety about India’s alignment with the United States. Meanwhile, because of the expected limitation to India’s cooperation with the U.S. on the latter’s competition with China, it also considerably decreases India’s strategic appeal for China to pursue.
Once the strategic questions of India’s power status and its alignment choices are answered, China’s remaining choices concern tactical approaches. With diplomatic engagement and maneuvering ongoing, China is most confident in the supply chain dependence it has built up vis-à-vis India. articles.summary: Kyrgyz president, Armenian premier discuss trade, transport, mountain preservation  A News
articles.full_text:
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan met in Yerevan to discuss strengthening bilateral relations through trade, transport, and environmental cooperation, and anticipated more regular high-level contacts.
- World
- Anadolu Agency
- Published Date: 12:09 PM 17 October 2026
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov met with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan in Yerevan on Saturday to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral ties, including expanding trade, improving transport and logistics links, and opening new trade routes.
The two leaders also discussed environmental protection and the preservation of mountain ecosystems, according to the Kyrgyz presidency.
Zhaparov invited Pashinyan to attend the second Global Mountain Summit, "Bishkek+25," scheduled to take place in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek in October 2027.
Pashinyan, on his part, expressed confidence that Zhaparov's first official visit to Armenia would open a new chapter in bilateral relations.
He also said the two sides reaffirmed their commitment to regular high-level contacts and closer cooperation between their foreign ministries and relevant government agencies, state news agency Armenpress reported.
He said they also discussed peace, stability, and security in the South Caucasus and Central Asia.
Education, science, technology, and youth development were also identified as areas for cooperation. The leaders agreed to promote exchanges of students, lecturers, and researchers, as well as joint educational programs and research initiatives.
Zhaparov arrived in Armenia on Thursday for a three-day visit to attend the Leaders' Summit held as part of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17).

articles.summary: Chinese premier says China ready to strengthen alignment of development strategies with Uzbekistan  People's Daily Online
articles.full_text:
Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Shen Hong)
TASHKENT, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Saturday that China stands ready to strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Uzbekistan and deepen cooperation in energy and resources, artificial intelligence, modern agriculture and other areas.
Li, who is on an official visit to the Central Asian country, made the remarks when holding talks with Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev met in August, charting the course for further development of bilateral relations, Li said.
Noting that next year marks the 35th anniversary of bilateral relations, Li said that China is ready to take this opportunity with Uzbekistan to carry forward their traditional friendship, deepen political mutual trust, enhance practical cooperation, and deepen the building of the China-Uzbekistan community with a shared future, so as to deliver greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Li said that China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to further leverage the complementary strengths of the two economies, continuously enhance connectivity in infrastructure, finance and other areas, advance the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, and strive for more tangible outcomes.
China is also willing to import more high-quality and specialty products from Uzbekistan, and welcomes Uzbekistan to make full use of platforms such as the China International Import Expo to actively explore the Chinese market, he added.
Li encouraged the two sides to continue to make good use of the mutual visa exemption policy, expand two-way personnel exchanges, strengthen exchanges and cooperation in culture, tourism, education, youth, locality and other fields, and constantly enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the two peoples.
China stands ready to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Uzbekistan within multilateral frameworks such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the China-Central Asia mechanism and the United Nations, work with all parties to implement the four global initiatives, and advance an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, he said.
For his part, Aripov said that Uzbekistan admires China's remarkable achievements in development, and sincerely appreciates China's strong support for Uzbekistan's reform and development efforts.
Under the joint guidance of the two heads of state, Uzbekistan-China relations have continued to reach new heights, he noted.
Aripov said that Uzbekistan is willing to work with China to fully promote the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and other projects of Belt and Road cooperation, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in economic and trade investment, agriculture, energy and mineral resources, customs, finance, digital technology, artificial intelligence, ecological protection and other fields, strengthen exchanges in tourism, education, locality and other fields, enhance multilateral coordination, and promote continuous development of the Uzbekistan-China all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era.
Before the talks, the two leaders jointly watched a video showcasing practical cooperation between China and Uzbekistan across various fields.
Following the talks, they witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering trade and economy, education, customs, health and poverty reduction, among other areas. During the visit, the two sides also signed cooperation documents on e-commerce, climate and media, among other fields.
On Saturday afternoon, Li also laid a wreath at the Independence Monument.

articles.full_text:
By Professor Maurice Okoli, Ph.D*
This article was first published in Eurasia Review.
MOSCOW | 17 October 2026 (IDN) — Perhaps, BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), with the new members and partner states, summit in New Delhi, from 11 September to 13, produced a new round of significant declarations, adapting its collective policy toward an increasingly emerging architecture, while distinctively building an ‘Asian model’ of economic alliance. Under India’s chairmanship, the summit focused on building a reputation that has been developing for nearly two decades. The timing was, particularly, notable. The most important strategic message was coined: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.”
Addressing the BRICS summit of leading developing nations in New Delhi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi warned that rising geopolitical tensions could increasingly affect people worldwide and called for deepening cooperation and strengthening support across the Global South. “The number of conflicts and tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and this is having an increasingly negative and far-reaching impact on the lives of ordinary people,” Modi said, alongside leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. That was one of the main messages sent across the world. Founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, BRICS has expanded to 11 members representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. It has sought greater representation for developing countries in global institutions and promoted alternative actions to Western-dominated financial systems. Pasted markdown
Geopolitics: Is BRICS Challenging the West?
BRICS leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration, expressing deep concern about forging consensus on many strategic questions, backing greater use of local currencies in trade and stronger cross-border payment systems, and calling for cooperation on food security, energy, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, and climate action. The declaration was a significant breakthrough, but it also reflects competing positions on key regional and geopolitical issues, posing a complex diplomatic challenge amid ongoing conflicts and heightened geopolitical tensions. It emphasises collective support for a multipolar world order and operational and structural reforms at the United Nations, including its Security Council, as well as global financial institutions such as the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The declaration showed that BRICS can move together and act on multilateral economic cooperation, and that this cooperation is sustainable in the Global South. This raises the question of whether India has used its presidency to push the BRICS grouping to become more capable of economic action, with reports indicating that India entered the role with more than just a diplomatic presence. For instance, during the financial year 2024-25, its total exports amounted to approximately $825 billion, with services accounting for an estimated $387 billion. Few developing countries can match New Delhi’s economic leverage, which stems from its large domestic market, expanding digital economy, and sustainable growth. Despite national preferences and differences among BRICS members, India is a major provider of digital public infrastructure, and its demography plays an increasingly important role in global consumption, production, and services. It therefore shows that BRICS members must build economic prosperity by opening doors. This new phase must strategically focus on broader economic leverage. Appropriately, India’s geography provides an additional layer of economic leverage, serving as a classic example for other Asian countries. Pasted markdown
Сorporate Economic Weight, Limited Collective Power
While BRICS’s economic weight is enormous, its ability to wield it collectively is not, some analysts argue. However, experts’ arguments closely connected to BRICS operational successes and achievements should not only be measured by whether it can pose an alternative to multinational institutions, but also whether it could make any noticeable difference, in terms of using its natural resources to increase regional trade, raise economic production and improve distribution across the Global South. Several experts portray BRICS as offering its member countries alternative pathways for channelling trade and investment that serve the collective interests of member countries–largely national development and poverty alleviation.
Meanwhile, scholars have reminded that BRICS emerged after the 2008 financial collapse and the failures of the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) Doha Round–trade negotiations aimed at reforming the international trading system in favour of Global South countries. Why would the BRICS want to take on the global governance responsibilities of the G7 members? This remains the central question among scholars today. However, many believe BRICS is more concerned with reforms and greater autonomy than with overthrowing the unravelling liberal international order. Pasted markdown
BRICS+ Financial Architecture
The group is noticeably dominated by China, which has the largest share of the group’s GDP, accounting for about 70% of the organisation’s total. The financial architecture of BRICS is made up of the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA). These components were signed into a treaty in 2014 and became active in 2015. The New Development Bank (NDB), formerly the BRICS Development Bank, is a multilateral development bank operated by the five BRICS states. Non-members can contribute to the NDB.
The bank primarily lends to infrastructure projects, with authorised lending of up to $34 billion annually. South Africa hosts the bank’s African headquarters. The bank started with $50 billion in capital, which grew to $100 billion over time. Records show Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa initially contributed $10 billion each, bringing the total to $50 billion. As of 2020, it had 53 projects underway worth around $15 billion. By 2025, the bank had approved more than $32 billion for 96 projects.
In 2021, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Uruguay joined the NDB during India’s 2026 presidency, which was estimated to be comprehensive and promising for BRICS, as India has outlined its framework of priorities, as it did during its G20 presidency several years ago. In close coordination with members and partner states within BRICS, India has balanced multifaceted interests and built mutual trust in the multipolar world system. The goal of transforming into a full-fledged international organisation must go beyond addressing current geopolitical challenges; it must also develop effective ways to engage in global development that reflect multipolarity. Today, BRICS collectively accounts for more than a quarter of the global economy and nearly half the world’s population. Pasted markdown
BRICS Advocates for Reforms at Financial Institutions
Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of BRICS countries have called for reform of global developmental financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, seeking a stronger voice for emerging market economies. “We will continue to strengthen coordination among BRICS members to make international financial institutions more representative, transparent and accountable. With the growing share of emerging market and developing economies in global output and growth, reform of global economic governance remains a consistent BRICS priority,” Finance Chiefs of BRICS countries underlined in an official joint statement.
“We continue to have serious concerns with the unilateral imposition of trade and finance-related actions, including the raising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, which distort trade and are inconsistent with World Trade Organisation rules,” the statement said. “We encourage the BRICS Payment Task Force to continue discussions, building on the ongoing work, to facilitate practical solutions for cross-border payments among BRICS countries, which are fast, low-cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent, and safe,” the statement said. While acknowledging the work of the BRICS payment task force, the finance chiefs pushed for greater interoperability of payment systems across member nations. It also noted that India will push for progress on linking digital currencies across BRICS countries. Pasted markdown
BRICS-Africa Transitioning from Diplomacy to Strategic Economy
South Africa (2010), Ethiopia, and Egypt (2024), as fully-fledged BRICS members, seem to be shifting from a policy of strategic ambiguity to a kind of assertive flexibility. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt are also positioning themselves as leading African voices for the Global South while, at the same time, maintaining relationships with competing Western powers. In principle, Africa generally collaborates with the United States and Asia-Pacific partners while, to a certain degree, striking multifaceted ties with Russia, and operates within the framework of the BRICS domain.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of the Arab Republic of Egypt held separate conversations on the current status and prospects for their relations, and further discussed ways of strengthening BRICS strategic partnership in politics and security, economics and finance, and cultural and humanitarian ties, while exchanging divergent views on current international and regional issues that are of common significance to global development. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt, however, plan to take new initiatives to improve and strengthen relations within BRICS.

articles.title: Chinese premier says China ready to strengthen alignment of development strategies with Uzbekistan - English.gov.cn
articles.summary: Chinese premier says China ready to strengthen alignment of development strategies with Uzbekistan  English.gov.cn
articles.full_text:
TASHKENT, Oct. 17 -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Saturday that China stands ready to strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Uzbekistan and deepen cooperation in energy and resources, artificial intelligence, modern agriculture and other areas.
Li, who is on an official visit to the Central Asian country, made the remarks when holding talks with Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev met in August, charting the course for further development of bilateral relations, Li said.
Noting that next year marks the 35th anniversary of bilateral relations, Li said that China is ready to take this opportunity with Uzbekistan to carry forward their traditional friendship, deepen political mutual trust, enhance practical cooperation, and deepen the building of the China-Uzbekistan community with a shared future, so as to deliver greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Li said that China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to further leverage the complementary strengths of the two economies, continuously enhance connectivity in infrastructure, finance and other areas, advance the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, and strive for more tangible outcomes.
China is also willing to import more high-quality and specialty products from Uzbekistan, and welcomes Uzbekistan to make full use of platforms such as the China International Import Expo to actively explore the Chinese market, he added.
Li encouraged the two sides to continue to make good use of the mutual visa exemption policy, expand two-way personnel exchanges, strengthen exchanges and cooperation in culture, tourism, education, youth, locality and other fields, and constantly enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the two peoples.
China stands ready to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Uzbekistan within multilateral frameworks such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the China-Central Asia mechanism and the United Nations, work with all parties to implement the four global initiatives, and advance an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, he said.
For his part, Aripov said that Uzbekistan admires China's remarkable achievements in development, and sincerely appreciates China's strong support for Uzbekistan's reform and development efforts.
Under the joint guidance of the two heads of state, Uzbekistan-China relations have continued to reach new heights, he noted.
Aripov said that Uzbekistan is willing to work with China to fully promote the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and other projects of Belt and Road cooperation, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in economic and trade investment, agriculture, energy and mineral resources, customs, finance, digital technology, artificial intelligence, ecological protection and other fields, strengthen exchanges in tourism, education, locality and other fields, enhance multilateral coordination, and promote continuous development of the Uzbekistan-China all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era.
Before the talks, the two leaders jointly watched a video showcasing practical cooperation between China and Uzbekistan across various fields.
Following the talks, they witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering trade and economy, education, customs, health and poverty reduction, among other areas. During the visit, the two sides also signed cooperation documents on e-commerce, climate and media, among other fields.
On Saturday afternoon, Li also laid a wreath at the Independence Monument.

articles.title: Why Central Asia should rely on India over China - dailyasianage.com
articles.summary: Why Central Asia should rely on India over China  dailyasianage.com
articles.full_text:
The world is entering a post-unipolar era, where sturdy bilateral trade and diplomatic ties are becoming increasingly indispensable amid growing geopolitical uncertainties. Nations are actively making choices to forge, resuscitate, or strengthen ties with the major emerging centres of power. The decision to forge or strengthen ties with the emerging powers is determined by various factors, including but not limited to geographical proximity, historical ties, current diplomatic requirements, and trade opportunities.
A similar situation has arisen in Central Asia. With the weakening dominance of Russia in the region, it has become an important arena for forging strategic ties for other regional powers, namely India and China. In the post-Moscow era, marked by the reduced influence of Russia in the region due to its weakening involvement in meeting regional investment, infrastructure, and security needs, the Central Asian nations are diversifying their strategic ties by building closer relations with China and India.
China has been a seasoned regional player as an infrastructure supplier, leveraging infrastructural initiatives like the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) for strategic ties, along with investments in transport, regional energy reserves, and digital infrastructure. On the other hand, India’s engagement has been driven by an issue-based development approach, often envisaged via the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the Chabahar Port, which are crucial to its Connect Central Asia policy, along with promoting thematic partnerships on rare earth metals and digital partnerships.
Given the involvement of the two emerging powers in the region, while adopting a multi-vector diplomacy, there are several compelling reasons for why Central Asian Republics (CARs) should tilt towards New Delhi on the trade and commerce front. First, the geostrategic and security concerns with respect to China’s BRI have made the region especially fertile for Indian engagement. Post 2015, India has viewed CAR as a single geographical unit for facilitating cooperation. Since then, multiple deals have been signed between India and CARs on a variety of issues, including security, energy, trade, and culture. As mentioned earlier, this rejuvenation of ties is also determined by the historicity of traditional and socioeconomic ties between the two.
Second, there exists anti-China sentiment and deep scepticism amongst the CARs for a variety of reasons. Central Asians are sceptical of Chinese investments, as these investments are considered risky and a threat to sovereignty. Besides, the Chinese treatment of ethnic minorities like the Uyghurs, Kazakhs and Kyrgyz has fuelled public angst. Chinese tendencies are often seen as expansionist, based on historical experiences. This is where the narrative of deep, friendly historical ties with India, and its influence as a soft cultural power, pitches in. India’s trade model with CARs focuses on sustainable infrastructure, low-interest lines of credit, and transparent frameworks. This eliminates the fears of debt-trap diplomacy. As a result, the CARs should build economic capabilities with India, as such engagement doesn’t risk their national sovereignty and ensures growth based on mutual respect.
Third, India is in the process of finalising the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between India and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Once signed, India will have direct access to the region’s huge hydrocarbon resources as well as open doors to the Eurasian markets. India also acts as a strong trade partner for Central Asia as it operates through a cooperative, non-exploitative model focused on affordable goods, digital growth, and strategic balance rather than overwhelming debt or economic dominance. Given that CARs heavily depend on Beijing for energy exports, this creates asymmetric leverage. Here, New Delhi acts as a critical diversification outlet through projects like the Chabahar Port and the INSTC; the CARs gain direct maritime access to the Indian Ocean and global markets, bypassing restrictive land routes.
India, with its booming pharmaceutical sector, also provides high-quality, affordable generic medicines and healthcare infrastructure, directly lowering public health expenditures across CARs. Moreover, going beyond the focus on resource extraction, India has been partnering with Central Asia through the Digital Partnership Forum, IT training, higher education scholarships, and healthcare cooperation.
Given the Indian Prime Minister’s visit to Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, and participation in the SCO Summit, the Connect Central Asia policy is being complemented by closer government-to-government ties and purposeful actions to translate policies into practice.
India and Central Asian nations have also been collaborating on safe, secure, and trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, building on frameworks established during events like the India AI Impact Summit. Though the trade between the two is around $2 billion, it leaves a vast room for growth through improved connectivity and sector diversification. There exists immense scope for trade between the two in trade in mineral fuels like oil, natural gas, and key minerals like aluminium and uranium (like long-term uranium supplies from Uzbekistan), along with cooperation extending to renewable electricity and hydropower production. This is accompanied by the possibility to expand trade in traditional sectors like agricultural trade, agribusiness, and food production. New Delhi has already signed the Strategic Partnership Agreements (SPA) with three of the five CARs (Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan), to stimulate defence cooperation and strengthen the trade ties.  
Central Asia’s growing collaboration with India is bound to bring a collaborative growth framework, bolstered by historical ties and respect for sovereignty.  On the trade front, India offers CARs a high-value partnership focused on sustainable economic development, tech transfer, and vital trade diversification. This is in contrast to China’s resource-extractive model, where the region is treated as a source for raw materials and a market for cheap manufactured goods. India stands to fill a crucial developmental gap through the supply of world-class pharmaceuticals, technical expertise, and digital infrastructure like digital payment systems, along with trade infrastructure via the INSTC and Chabahar Port, to provide the economies access to global markets. In the post-Russia CARs, West Asia should strengthen its ties with India as it is a reliable trade partner; Strong ties with New Delhi prevent CARs excessive economic dependency on Beijing while ensuring that commerce with India builds local capacities and safeguards CARs’ economic sovereignty.
Written By: Sun Lee (The author is a pseudonym for a writer who covers Asia and geopolitical affairs.)

articles.title: Kazakhstan, Cambodia Seek AI Cooperation and Stronger Trade Ties - The Astana Times
articles.summary: Kazakhstan, Cambodia Seek AI Cooperation and Stronger Trade Ties  The Astana Times
articles.full_text:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Cambodia are looking to expand cooperation in artificial intelligence, energy, agriculture and trade, while exploring direct air links, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet held talks on Oct. 17.
The discussions marked the first visit to Kazakhstan by a Cambodian prime minister and came as the two countries mark 32 years of diplomatic relations. Tokayev said the visit could open a new chapter in bilateral ties, with both countries seeking to translate shared intentions into practical cooperation, Akorda reported.
“Kazakhstan considers Cambodia a reliable partner in Southeast Asia and an important link in expanding our partnership with ASEAN countries,” Tokayev said during the expanded-format talks.
He added that the countries would adopt a joint statement outlining their shared vision for future relations and sign several bilateral documents.
AI and digital government
Technology emerged as a key area for cooperation, with Tokayev highlighting opportunities in artificial intelligence and digital government. Hun Manet and his delegation were scheduled to visit the Alem.ai International Center to learn about Kazakhstan’s AI initiatives and technological developments.
Tokayev noted Kazakhstan’s progress in the United Nations E-Government Development Index and said the two countries could achieve significant results by combining mutual interest with political commitment.
“I am convinced that, given mutual interest and firm political will, we can achieve significant progress in expanding cooperation across many areas of mutual interest,” he said.
The two leaders also discussed energy cooperation. During their one-on-one meeting earlier in the day, Tokayev proposed exploring direct air links to facilitate tourism and people-to-people exchanges.
“Many Kazakh people would like to visit Cambodia and discover its attractions. We need to discuss the possibility of establishing direct air links between our countries,” Tokayev said.
Trade, agriculture and education
Hun Manet expressed Cambodia’s interest in expanding cooperation in food security, agriculture and manufacturing, alongside energy and digitalization.
He also emphasized the longstanding humanitarian ties between the countries, noting that more than 120 Cambodian students had studied in Kazakhstan. Many have since taken up senior positions in public administration, including as provincial governors, state secretaries and ministry officials.
“Our countries are connected by a shared history and strong people-to-people ties,” Hun Manet said.
Tokayev praised Cambodia’s socioeconomic progress and expressed support for its long-term development goals under Cambodia Vision 2050 and the Pentagonal Strategy.
The leaders also highlighted their constructive political dialogue and engagement at the international level, including through their respective permanent missions to the United Nations. Tokayev commended Cambodia’s support for Kazakhstan’s initiatives on several topics on the UN General Assembly agenda.
Both officials expressed confidence that the talks would help increase bilateral trade, strengthen business ties and create new opportunities for partnership.
In the presence of Tokayev and Hun Manet, the two sides exchanged six memorandums of understanding covering cooperation in artificial intelligence and digital development, digital government and information and communication technologies, trade and economic relations, culture and the arts, and tourism. The documents also established sister-city relations between Astana and Phnom Penh.
Earlier, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos Kanat Tumysh told The Astana Times that the countries were seeking to expand trade, explore investment opportunities and strengthen transport and technology cooperation.

articles.title: US To Make Investment, Counterterrorism Push As Rubio Heads To Central Asia - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: US To Make Investment, Counterterrorism Push As Rubio Heads To Central Asia  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON -- As Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to Uzbekistan this weekend, Washington is hoping the high-level diplomatic engagement translates into concrete economic and security cooperation.
Speaking to reporters on a background call on October 16 Rubio's visit, a State Department official said more than 200 American companies would accompany the secretary to Samarkand, where he is expected to meet with the foreign ministers of all five Central Asian countries.
The tour reflects the Trump administration's effort to combine diplomacy with trade, investment, and security cooperation across South and Central Asia, regions Washington views as increasingly important to its economic and strategic interests.
"For too long, the United States has focused on the Middle East and the East, and this area in the middle, Central Asia, has not gotten the attention that it deserves," the senior official said.
SEE ALSO:
Rubio Heads To Central Asia As US Seeks Bigger Role In Region Dominated By Russia, China
The American delegation will include representatives of major companies such as Boeing, Citibank, and Franklin Templeton, as well as businesses operating in critical minerals and other strategic sectors.
Officials from the US International Development Finance Corporation, the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the National Security Council, and the State Department will also participate in meetings designed to connect American businesses with potential partners across Central Asia.
The senior State Department official said Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan alone had generated more than $30 billion in new investments into the United States over the past year.
Republican Senator John Curtis, who has supported closer US engagement with Central Asia, says the region's stability is essential to American interests at a time of heightened uncertainty elsewhere in the world.
"A stable Central Asian region, with so much uncertainty in other parts of the globe, is just essential for us," he told RFE/RL.
"It's up to them, but to partner with us could be an incredibly important part of a relationship. As everybody knows, critical minerals are very important, not just to the United States but to the world. And I think that's a great asset they have that could be very important."
Samarkand, a historic trading center on the Silk Road, will serve as the main venue for the Central Asian portion of Rubio's trip.
SEE ALSO:
As Russian Arms Exports Slide, Central Asia Shops Elsewhere
The visit will include bilateral meetings and the C5+1 format meeting, as well as direct engagement between American companies, regional businesses, and government representatives.
Kazakhstan's announced intention to join the Abraham Accords was another key development highlighted during the briefing. The senior official said Washington was working toward a potential signing ceremony but did not provide a date.
“Stay tuned," the official said, adding that the sides hoped to complete the process "sooner than later.”
The Abraham Accords were originally established to normalize relations between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority countries.
Kazakhstan's potential participation would extend the framework's reach, although the official did not provide details about the terms or timing of the country's formal accession.
The official also said Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan had been invited to attend the Group of 20 summit as observers for the first time.
The invitations were presented as part of Washington's broader effort to raise Central Asia's international profile and deepen ties with its governments.

articles.title: Beyond The Eurasian Economic Union: Why Central Asia Needs A Common Market – OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Beyond The Eurasian Economic Union: Why Central Asia Needs A Common Market – OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The article argues that the Eurasian Economic Union has failed to deliver equitable free movement of goods, capital, and labor because of Russia’s dominant position, selective rule application, customs delays, and recurring disputes involving Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Armenia.
- It proposes a Central Asian common market that would simplify customs, reduce non-tariff barriers, improve transport connectivity (including the Middle Corridor), and pool the region’s energy, mineral, and agricultural resources to strengthen collective bargaining power.
- Broader ideas such as the Silk Seven Plus framework (potentially including Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan) are presented as ways to diversify routes toward southern seaports, though success would require political stability, infrastructure investment, and sustained prioritization of regional over short-term interests.
Central Asia is entering a critical phase in its economic and geopolitical evolution. For decades, the region’s economic relationships have been shaped by its historical connections with Russia, inherited trade networks, and dependence on external markets. The establishment of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) in 2015 was presented as a significant step towards regional integration, promising the free movement of goods, capital, and labour among its members. However, persistent trade restrictions, political disagreements, and unequal power relations have increasingly exposed the limitations of this framework.
As Central Asian countries seek to diversify their economic partnerships and strengthen their strategic autonomy, the idea of a regional common market deserves greater attention. Such an arrangement could enable the countries of Central Asia to deepen intra-regional trade, coordinate infrastructure development, and negotiate more effectively with international partners. Moving beyond existing arrangements would not simply be an economic adjustment; it could also represent a broader effort to establish a more independent regional identity.
The EAEU was envisioned as an economic integration project capable of creating a common commercial space across Eurasia. Under Russian leadership, it sought to facilitate trade, improve labour mobility, and strengthen economic cooperation among participating states. Yet its implementation has frequently fallen short of these objectives. Rather than functioning consistently as a partnership among equals, the organisation has faced criticism over Russia’s dominant position and the selective application of its economic rules. For Armenia, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan, membership has not eliminated the barriers that complicate cross-border commerce. Customs delays, restrictions on exports, and disagreements over regulatory policies have undermined the principle of an integrated market. These problems raise questions about whether the EAEU can deliver the economic predictability and mutual benefits that its members initially expected.
Recent disputes illustrate the growing tensions between the EAEU’s formal commitments and the economic policies pursued by its members. Kyrgyzstan, for instance, has challenged Russia over the treatment of migrant workers, particularly in relation to social protection and healthcare rights. Disagreements over export restrictions have also demonstrated that member states remain willing to adopt measures that conflict with the spirit of free trade. Kazakhstan has encountered similar difficulties in its economic relationship with Russia. Disputes over vehicle imports, domestic agricultural markets, and cross-border movement have highlighted the vulnerability of regional trade to unilateral policy decisions.
Delays at the Kazakh-Russian border have also disrupted transportation, demonstrating how administrative and security-related measures can undermine the benefits of economic integration. Armenia’s growing dissatisfaction with Moscow has added another dimension to these challenges. Its consideration of alternative economic and political partnerships reflects a broader debate about the costs and benefits of remaining within a Russia-centred framework. Collectively, these developments suggest that formal membership in a regional organisation does not automatically guarantee equitable treatment or uninterrupted commerce.
A Central Asian common market could provide a more regionally grounded alternative to the limitations of the EAEU. Rather than depending on an external power to determine the direction of economic cooperation, participating countries could develop common rules based on their shared interests and national priorities. The immediate objective would be to simplify customs procedures, reduce non-tariff barriers, improve transport connectivity, and establish predictable conditions for businesses operating across national borders. Greater regulatory coordination could reduce the costs of moving goods and make regional supply chains more efficient. Such integration would also allow Central Asian countries to make better use of their complementary economic resources. The region possesses substantial energy reserves, critical minerals, agricultural potential, and strategic geographical advantages. Individually, national markets may have limited bargaining power in negotiations with major international economies. Collectively, however, they could offer investors a larger and more connected commercial environment.
Transport connectivity would be central to the success of a common market. Central Asia’s landlocked geography has historically increased transportation costs and limited direct access to global maritime trade. Improving regional connectivity could help overcome these constraints by linking production centres with international markets through more diversified routes. The Middle Corridor, which connects parts of Central Asia with the South Caucasus and onward to European markets, offers an important opportunity. Its effectiveness depends not only on physical infrastructure but also on coordinated customs procedures, efficient border crossings, reliable logistics, and compatible regulations. A common market could help participating countries plan investments collectively and reduce delays along the route. Regional coordination would also strengthen the ability of Central Asian governments to diversify their external economic relationships. Rather than relying disproportionately on established routes through Russia, they could develop alternative connections that improve resilience against geopolitical disruptions. However, such projects would require substantial investment, careful financial planning, and cooperation among the countries involved.
One proposal associated with broader regional integration is the Silk Seven Plus initiative. It envisages a framework centred on the five Central Asian states and Azerbaijan, with the possibility of incorporating Afghanistan and eventually Pakistan. Its geographical vision extends cooperation beyond Central Asia towards the Arabian Sea, potentially creating additional routes to international markets. The inclusion of southern transport connections could provide Central Asian exporters with greater access to Pakistan’s seaports. This would offer an alternative to established northern routes and create opportunities for expanded trade with South Asia and other global markets.
However, the initiative’s success would depend on political stability, infrastructure development, financing, and effective cross-border coordination. Afghanistan’s security and governance challenges, differences among participating economies, and the complexity of regional transport projects would all need to be addressed. Even so, the proposal reflects an important strategic principle: Central Asia’s economic future need not be confined to a single geopolitical or institutional framework. By developing multiple trade routes and partnerships, the region could increase its economic flexibility and reduce exposure to external disruptions.
A Central Asian common market could help translate the region’s shared economic interests into a coordinated development strategy. Through harmonised customs procedures, improved connectivity, stronger regional supply chains, and diversified trade partnerships, the five Central Asian states could enhance their collective bargaining power while preserving national sovereignty. The transition would not be easy, and a new framework would not automatically eliminate political disagreements or economic barriers. Its credibility would depend on practical implementation, transparent rules, and the willingness of governments to prioritise long-term regional interests over short-term political calculations.
