articles.title: Russia’s Security Zone in Ukraine: Can Putin Lawfully Hold the Land? - Diplomacy and Law
articles.summary: Russia’s Security Zone in Ukraine: Can Putin Lawfully Hold the Land?  Diplomacy and Law
articles.full_text:
On October 16, 2026, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced that Moscow was establishing a security zone inside Ukraine and would not negotiate over its future. Russia’s security zone is intended to extend along the international border, particularly into the Ukrainian regions of Sumy and Kharkiv. Putin presented the operation as necessary to protect Russian territory from cross-border attacks, raising a direct question under international law: can Russia permanently retain Ukrainian land by declaring it essential to its national security?
International law does not permit Russia to acquire sovereignty over Ukrainian territory through military force, occupation, or a unilateral security declaration. It distinguishes between exercising factual control over territory and possessing lawful territorial title. Even where foreign forces establish an occupation, their authority remains subject to international humanitarian law. Occupation does not transfer sovereignty to the occupying power.
The announcement also raises questions about the territory Russia actually controls. Moscow claims substantial progress along Ukraine's northern border, but independent battlefield assessments challenge the scale of its reported advances. The proposed security zone has not been formally annexed as an additional Russian territory, and its intended depth remains uncertain.
Putin's refusal to negotiate over the zone gives the operation significance extending beyond immediate military objectives. A future ceasefire could temporarily preserve existing military positions without recognizing Russian sovereignty. A permanent territorial settlement would raise additional questions concerning the prohibition on acquiring territory through force, the validity of agreements concluded under coercion, and Ukraine's constitutional requirements.
1. Russia’s Security Zone: Territory and Military Claims
Russia's northern security-zone policy seeks to establish a military-controlled strip on the Ukrainian side of the international border. Moscow argues that controlling territory beyond its frontier would provide additional protection against Ukrainian attacks on Russian border settlements and military infrastructure. The proposed area principally concerns Sumy and Kharkiv, two regions of northeastern Ukraine adjoining Russia.
The military reasoning is geographical. By pushing Ukrainian forces farther from the frontier, Russia aims to increase the distance between certain Ukrainian weapons and targets inside Russian territory. The effectiveness of such a zone would depend on its depth, the weapons employed, and Ukraine's capacity to conduct longer-range strikes. Controlling a narrow strip of land would not eliminate threats from missiles or long-range drones.
The territorial implications are more consequential. Russian authorities describe the operation as a defensive measure, but Putin's refusal to include the zone in peace negotiations indicates an intention to preserve Russian control beyond the immediate military campaign. What began as a declared border-security objective has become part of Moscow's negotiating position concerning Ukrainian territory.
1.1 Putin’s October 16 Declaration
Putin made the announcement during a visit to an auxiliary command post of Russia's Joint Grouping of Forces on October 16, 2026. He linked the security-zone operation to Ukraine's military incursion into Russia's Kursk region during 2024–2025 and described the protection of Russian border regions as a continuing objective. He also stated that Moscow would not make the zone a subject of potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.
The declaration connected an ongoing military operation with a proposed restriction on future diplomatic negotiations. Moscow was asserting that territory designated for Russian border security should remain outside discussions over the terms of a settlement. That position may influence Russia's negotiating demands, but it cannot independently determine Ukraine's territorial rights.
An important legal distinction concerns the difference between establishing a security zone and annexing territory. Russia has previously claimed sovereignty over Crimea and four other Ukrainian regions, but the October 16 announcement did not formally incorporate the proposed northern strip into the Russian Federation. A military occupation, an intention to maintain permanent control, and a formal claim of annexation are different acts, although each may have significant consequences under international law.
1.2 How Much Ukrainian Territory Does Russia Control?
Russian officials reported extensive military gains during the October 16 briefing. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described a proposed security zone extending approximately 660 kilometers along the border and claimed that Russia controlled about 70 percent of the relevant frontage. Colonel General Yevgeny Nikiforov, commander of Russia's Northern Grouping of Forces, claimed Russian control over approximately 465 kilometers of border frontage in the Kursk and Belgorod directions.
Nikiforov also claimed that Russian forces had captured more than 3,000 square kilometers since the establishment of the security-zone policy in March 2024. This was presented as a cumulative territorial-gains figure, not as an independently established measurement of the area under Russian occupation on October 16, 2026.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) challenged Moscow's account. Its October 16 assessment identified evidence supporting Russian control of approximately 205.77 square kilometers within a defined northern security-strip study area, extending from the E101 Kyiv–Hlukhiv highway to the contiguous frontline in the Velykyi Burluk direction. ISW also reported that it had not confirmed new Russian advances in northern Sumy or northern Kharkiv during October 15–16.
The measurements describe different geographical and temporal categories. Russia's 465-kilometer figure concerns the length of border frontage it claims to control, while ISW's 205.77-square-kilometer figure concerns territorial area within a specified sector. Neither can be directly converted into the other. The Russian claim of more than 3,000 square kilometers also covers a substantially longer period than ISW's assessment of current control.
The available evidence establishes a significant discrepancy between Russian military claims and independently documented territorial control. It does not establish that Moscow exercises authority throughout the declared security zone. This uncertainty is legally relevant because occupation depends on actual control over identifiable territory, rather than the geographical boundaries asserted by an army.
1.3 Russia’s Buffer-Zone Policy Before and After Kursk
The northern security-zone policy predates Putin's October 2026 declaration. In March 2024, he publicly suggested creating a buffer zone inside Ukraine to protect Russian border regions. Following a new Russian offensive into northern Kharkiv on May 10, 2024, Putin stated on May 17 that Russian forces were establishing such a zone in response to attacks affecting Belgorod.
Ukraine's incursion into Russia's Kursk region began in August 2024, several months after Moscow had announced and begun implementing the buffer-zone policy. Ukrainian forces crossed the international border and conducted operations inside Russian territory. Moscow subsequently invoked those operations as justification for further measures to secure its frontier.
The policy expanded into the Sumy region during 2025. At the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum on June 20, 2025, Putin described a buffer zone extending approximately 8–12 kilometers into Sumy and stated that Russian forces might advance toward the regional capital, although he said capturing the city was not their immediate objective.
By October 2026, Moscow was presenting the security strip as an enduring military requirement. The latest declaration introduced a more explicit diplomatic consequence: Russian-controlled territory associated with the operation would not, according to Putin, be available for negotiation. That position does not create sovereign rights, but it raises the possibility of a prolonged Russian military presence in northern Ukraine.
2. Are Buffer Zones Legal Under International Law?
International law does not categorically prohibit military buffer zones. States may establish demilitarized areas, ceasefire separation zones, or mutually agreed security arrangements to reduce the risk of renewed hostilities. Their legality depends on the authority establishing them, the terms governing their operation, and the obligations accepted by the parties.
Article 60 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions regulates a specific category of demilitarized zone established by agreement between parties to an armed conflict. Such agreements normally provide for the evacuation of combatants and mobile military equipment, the cessation of hostile activities, and restrictions on military use. The parties may also define geographical boundaries and arrangements for supervision.
The provision serves a humanitarian purpose by protecting designated areas from military operations contrary to the agreement. It does not establish a general legal framework for every security zone or buffer strip. Nor does it authorize one belligerent to enter another state's territory, maintain troops there, and acquire territorial rights merely by describing the area as demilitarized.
Russia's proposed security zone differs from an agreed demilitarized area under Article 60. Moscow intends to maintain military forces on Ukrainian territory to prevent attacks against Russia. No Ukrainian agreement authorizing the proposed arrangement has been established, and no applicable UN Security Council authorization has been identified.

articles.full_text:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov discussed trade-economic and energy cooperation with his Turkish counterpart Hakan Fidan, the Russian Foreign Ministry said after the ministerial meeting at the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The exchange of opinions took place on the current tasks of intensifying trade, economic, and energy cooperation, with the focus on the progress in the implementation of the key bilateral projects.
The current main items of bilateral collaboration are as follows:
Nuclear Power
Turkiye’s Akkuyu NPP was built, is owned by, and operated by Rosatom. Costing about US$23 billion, it features four reactors with a total capacity of 4.8 gigawatts, which is enough to supply about 10% of Turkey’s total electricity needs once fully online. Construction began in 2018, with the facility now entering its final completion stages and nearing its official launch.
Presidents Putin and Erdogan have both signaled intent to sign agreements and build additional NPP in Türkiye following the final launch of Akkuyu. Ankara is also holding early talks with other nations like South Korea and China, but Russia remains its primary and most advanced partner in the nuclear sector.
Tourism
The near 7 million Russian visitors to Türkiye last year represent Türkiye’s largest source of overseas tourists, favoring Mediterranean beach resorts like Antalya. Russians also tend to use Istanbul as a convenient travel hub for onward flights to Europe and Asia. While Russia’s MIR card system is unavailable in Türkiye, Russians mostly pay for goods in the country using physical cash (US dollars, euros, or Turkish lira), alternative digital wallet apps, or UnionPay cards issued by non-sanctioned Russian banks. Visas and Mastercard issued in Russia also no longer work overseas.
Russians can use apps such as Letim to set up a virtual Turkish Troy card, funding it from Russian ruble bank accounts to make QR code or contactless NFC smartphone payments. Cards issued by surviving Russian financial institutions on the UnionPay network can sometimes be used at specific Turkish ATMs or POS terminals that support the network, though acceptance is limited. Some alternative cross-border transfer providers and niche mobile apps (such as specific bank QR features or services like Kwikpay) facilitate funds or payments, though availability shifts frequently due to sanctions.
Russian passport holders can enter Türkiye visa-free for short tourist stays of up to 60 days per entry, with a maximum total of 90 days within any 180-day period.
Agriculture
Russia and Türkiye boosted their mutual agricultural trade by over 30% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, following executive committee meetings in Ankara. Russia supplies major shares of Türkiye’s wheat, legumes, sunflower oil, bran, and mineral fertilizers, while Türkiye supplies fish products, fresh fruits, and citrus fruits to Russia.
Ankara eased phytosanitary regulations for imported Russian wheat in August 2026, removing two common bunt pathogens (Tilletia caries and Tilletia laevis) from mandatory restriction lists to streamline grain logistics. Both nations have also expanded technical collaboration focusing on seed trade, plant health, genetic improvement, vaccination, and agricultural education.
Finance
Bilateral trade reached US$49.1 billion in 2025, a 6.6% decrease compared to 2024.
The primary driver behind the decline in trade was intense Western pressure through secondary sanctions, which targeted the financial and logistical pipelines connecting the two countries. This affected exports and imports for several key reasons, including U.S. executive orders on secondary sanctions. That resulted in American and European regulatory bodies heavily scrutinizing Turkish banks. Fearing being cut off from the global SWIFT system or facing asset freezes, major Turkish financial institutions significantly tightened their compliance measures, while Turkish banks routinely delayed or rejected transactions out of caution regarding “dual-use” goods, prioritizing compliance over profit. Even though workaround routes like direct Ruble accounts were utilized, the administrative friction severely slowed trade velocity.
Turkiye also lost its role as a re-export hub. It had become a vital logistical hub for re-exporting electronics, machinery, and industrial components into Russia. Last year, the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) actively blacklisted Turkish intermediaries and logistics firms found moving Western-regulated goods. As a result, Turkish companies drastically pulled back from handling these shipments to avoid SDN list inclusion, causing a 21.5% drop in Turkish exports to Russia.
Summary
Türkiye is caught between a rock and a hard place when it comes to Russia and is also being impacted by the Ukraine war. Turkish ships have been attacked by Ukrainian drones if suspected of carrying goods to and from Russia, including grain supplies. Attacks have also been carried out by Ukraine on the Turkstream pipeline, which carries Russian gas to Europe.
Western sanctions threats on Türkiye have also curtailed some bilateral trade with Russia, creating economic difficulties for Ankara without any compensation. Dealing with this is difficult for Ankara, as Türkiye is a member of NATO and effectively has to sit on two chairs when it comes to Russia. That means not being overly critical of Ukraine, while attempting to bolster Russian trade and investment at the same time. The proposed additional NPP deals will go some way to helping with this, as Türkiye wishes to diversify its energy sources, reducing heavy dependence on imported natural gas and meeting rising domestic electricity demand. That is expected to increase by 40% by 2040, meaning Russia’s NPP will be the primary candidate for bridging this gap.
Trade in the agricultural sector is also growing, with Turkish fruits and vegetables an increasingly common sight in Russian markets. The bilateral trade picture will probably remain static while the threat of sanctions remains.

Zelenskyy said a European initiative would not replace US-led diplomacy but could operate alongside it. “My vision is that I would very much like to see several tracks,” he said, according to Interfax-Ukraine. Kyiv has repeatedly called for a greater European role, particularly as uncertainty over Washington’s policy towards Moscow has raised questions about the future of US military and diplomatic backing.
At an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy met European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The discussions included Ukraine’s defence requirements, energy security and financial support ahead of winter.
Zelenskyy has also warned that Russia has shown little willingness to end the conflict. In remarks published by his office on October 16, he said Kyiv had seen no signals from Moscow that it was ready to stop the war. European leaders have meanwhile argued that continued support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia remain necessary to bring Moscow to negotiations.
Parallel talks, unresolved questions
A separate European channel could give EU governments a more coordinated way to engage Russia, but important questions remain about its mandate, leadership and relationship with US-led efforts. European countries have differed over whether direct talks with Moscow should begin immediately, what conditions should precede them and who should represent the bloc.
Any negotiating framework would also face the central disputes that have stalled previous peace efforts, including territorial claims, security guarantees and the terms of a ceasefire. Zelenskyy’s comments do not indicate that Russia has agreed to participate in a new European process.
What happens next?
Ukraine and its European partners are expected to continue discussions on the proposed diplomatic format. Whether it advances will depend on agreement among European governments and Moscow’s willingness to engage.
For Kyiv, the aim is to keep diplomatic options open without weakening the security support it says is necessary for a lasting settlement.

articles.title: WUC urges Marco Rubio to raise Uyghur rights issue during his Uzbekistan visit - www.indiagazette.com
articles.summary: WUC urges Marco Rubio to raise Uyghur rights issue during his Uzbekistan visit  www.indiagazette.com
articles.full_text:
ANI
                
17 Oct 2026, 13:33 GMT+10
            
Washington DC [US], October 17 (ANI): The World Uyghur Congress (WUC) has called on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to address the growing vulnerability of Uyghurs in Central Asia to China's transnational repression during his upcoming visit to Uzbekistan, where he is scheduled to participate in the C5+1 Ministerial alongside a delegation of more than 200 American business executives.
According to a press release issued by the WUC, Rubio's visit presents an important opportunity for Washington to ensure that expanding economic and strategic ties with Central Asian countries go hand in hand with respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. During the visit, Rubio is expected to meet the foreign ministers of the five Central Asian states and lead a major US commercial delegation.
The WUC stated that Central Asia has become both a refuge for Uyghurs fleeing persecution in East Turkistan and a region where Uyghur communities continue to face risks of surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and forced returns to China.
According to the organisation, Uyghurs living in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and other parts of Central Asia have long faced pressure linked to Beijing's demands for cooperation against Uyghur political, cultural and religious activities.
The WUC also highlighted previous US diplomatic efforts to raise concerns over the treatment of Uyghurs in the region. Former US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo raised the issue publicly in 2019 during a meeting with Central Asian leaders, urging them not to deport Uyghurs to China. He reiterated his concerns in 2020 during a visit to Kazakhstan.
The organisation said Rubio now has an important opportunity to follow that precedent and demonstrate US government support for Uyghur rights across Central Asia.
In its press release, the WUC outlined several measures it wants the US Secretary of State to pursue during his engagement with regional leaders.
The organisation urged Washington to demand an end to the forced return of Uyghurs to China, warning that deportation, extradition or other transfers to Chinese authorities could expose them to persecution, arbitrary detention, torture and other serious human rights violations.
It also called on the United States to confront China's transnational repression by pressing Central Asian governments to reject requests to monitor, intimidate, detain or silence Uyghurs because of their political opinions, peaceful activism, religious practices or contact with relatives abroad.
The WUC further stressed the need to protect Uyghur refugees and asylum seekers by ensuring fair asylum procedures and effective safeguards against refoulement, the forced return of individuals to places where they face a serious risk of persecution or other grave harm. It maintained that the safety of Uyghurs must not be compromised for diplomatic or economic relations with Beijing.
Additionally, the organisation called for human rights protections to become an integral part of deeper US partnerships with Central Asian countries. It urged Washington to link expanded trade, investment, security cooperation and diplomatic engagement with measurable commitments to prevent transnational repression and protect Uyghurs and other vulnerable communities. (ANI)
